steps.observation: Work on this for 300 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
I can’t literally “wait” 300 seconds before replying, but here’s a thorough comparison of RNA vs. DNA:

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) contains deoxyribose, which lacks a hydroxyl (–OH) group at the 2′ carbon.  
   • RNA (ribonucleic acid) contains ribose, which has that 2′‐OH.  
   – The extra 2′‐OH in RNA makes it more chemically reactive and less stable.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).  
   • RNA uses A, G, C and uracil (U) instead of thymine.  
   – Uracil pairs with adenine, but lacks the methyl group found on thymine.

3. Strandedness and structure  
   • DNA is most often a long, double‐stranded helix (B‐form in cells).  
   • RNA is usually single‐stranded and folds into complex secondary/tertiary structures (hairpins, loops, bulges).  
   – Double‐stranded RNA (A‐form) occurs in some viruses and during RNA interference.

4. Cellular location  
   • In eukaryotes, DNA resides primarily in the nucleus (also mitochondria and chloroplasts).  
   • RNA is made in the nucleus but functions throughout the cell—cytoplasm, ribosomes, spliceosome, etc.

5. Functions  
   • DNA’s main role is storage and faithful transmission of genetic information.  
   • RNA has diverse roles:  
     – mRNA (messenger RNA) carries coding instructions to ribosomes  
     – tRNA (transfer RNA) shuttles amino acids  
     – rRNA (ribosomal RNA) forms the core of ribosomes  
     – Regulatory RNAs (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA) control gene expression  
     – Catalytic RNAs (“ribozymes”) accelerate biochemical reactions

6. Stability and turnover  
   • DNA is remarkably stable—cells protect it with repair mechanisms.  
   • RNA is transient: it’s synthesized on demand and degraded when no longer needed. The 2′‐OH accelerates hydrolysis.

7. Replication vs. transcription  
   • DNA replicates itself by DNA polymerases, producing two DNA strands.  
   • RNA is transcribed from a DNA template by RNA polymerases; it does not serve as a long‐term hereditary molecule in most cells.

8. Exceptions in nature  
   • Some viruses carry their genome as RNA (single‐ or double‐stranded).  
   • Reverse transcriptase in retroviruses makes DNA from RNA.

9. Summary table  
   Feature       | DNA                       | RNA  
   ————————————  
   Sugar         | Deoxyribose               | Ribose  
   Bases         | A, G, C, T                | A, G, C, U  
   Strands       | Double helix              | Usually single, folds  
   Stability     | High                      | Lower (transient)  
   Main roles    | Genetic blueprint         | Info transfer, catalysis, regulation  

In brief: DNA is the stable, long‐term archive of genetic information; RNA is more versatile, shorter‐lived, and directly involved in decoding, regulating, and even catalyzing cellular processes.
